newsitem.title: CROATIA: Experts start exhuming new mass grave in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Experts start exhuming new mass grave in Croatia.

text.p: Croatian experts, working under international supervision, have begun exhuming a mass grave in Eastern Slavonia, an area notorious for atrocities in the 1991 Serb-Croat war, investigators said on Tuesday.

"The dig at a mass grave, believed to contain between 60 and 70 bodies, began in Lovas on Tuesday," Colonel Ivan Grujic, chief of the Croatian government commission for missing persons, told reporters at U.N. headquarters in Vukovar.

Vukovar, on the Danube River border with Serbia and capital of Eastern Slavonia, was demolished in a ferocious three-month siege by Yugoslav army regulars backing a local Serb minority revolt against Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia.

Croatian investigators, working under supervision of forensic experts from the International Criminal Tribunal on former Yugoslavia in The Hague (ICTY), have dug a trench 11 by three metres (yards) and already found 19 bodies.
"There is irrefutable evidence the victims met violent death," Grujic said.
He said all the victims, bar "one or two Serbs", were Croats but refused to reveal details, claiming the investigation was still going on.
Grujic said all of the victims were elderly civilians and there were roughly even numbers of men and women.
He said he expected the excavation of the grave believed to be almost 36 metres (yards) long to be completed next week when the bodies will be taken to Zagreb for identification.
"Then the victims will be given a proper burial in keeping with their religious beliefs," Grujic said.
"The goal of the investigation is also to gather evidence of war crimes in pursuit of war criminals," he said.
Lovas, a tiny village some 20 km (12 miles) southeast of the infamous Ovcara mass grave near Vukovar, was taken by Serb paramilitary forces on October 10, 1991.
Grujic said the victims were believed to have been killed in a period of eight days.
ICTY has indicted three former Yugoslav army officers for the killing of 261 Croat hospital patients seized in Vukovar after the town's fall to Serb forces in November 1991.
In a five-week exhumation completed on October 4, ICTY experts retrieved 200 bodies from Ovcara, where the patients were said by survivors and other witnesses to have been machine-gunned.
The massacre at Ovcara was among the most notorious in the bitter six-month war in 1991, but other mass tombs are believed to lie in Eastern Slavonia.
The Lovas mass grave is the 63rd to be dug up in Croatia, Grujic said.

Eastern Slavonia is administered by the United Nations, whose current mandate ends on July 15 when the area is due to come under Croatian government control. However the United States has hinted it might call for the current mandate covering 5,000 troops to be extended.
Croatia recaptured all other Serb-held territory in a lightning offensive in 1995 and Eastern Slavonia is now home to thousands of Serbs who fled their advance.
Each side has accused each other of committing war crimes and atrocities.
The war crimes tribunal in The Hague has indicted 75 people but mostly in connection with atrocities in neighbouring Bosnia.
